problem: VLN requires users to describe the full path in detail for every navigation session, which is costly. Prior work builds maps from images or geometric maps and uses language only as auxiliary information; none maps a space from natural-language path descriptions alone.
motivation: Ideally a user only names the destination and the robot reuses earlier path descriptions to produce a path. LLMs could parse textual paths, but they have weak long-term memory and spatial reasoning, so storing an implicit map in the prompt may fail to recombine paths.
key_idea: Use LLMs only to translate textual paths into a canonical representation (waypoints plus turn actions), build an explicit topological graph with per-node actions, and do path finding and action inference symbolically on that graph.
insight: LLMs are poor at recombining spatial structure from text: implicit-map combined-path success is 8-10% for shortest paths (GPT-4 reachable 44%), versus 92% for the explicit map. Delegating spatial reasoning to a symbolic graph with action algebra leaves only extraction errors, which are the remaining failures. The paper also reports that 96% of implicit-method failures were wrong rotation or direction.
method: Topological map with actions: graph G(N,E) with waypoints as nodes and stored actions at nodes, discretized by turn angle into Forward, Left, Right and Turn-around.
Canonical representation: an LLM converts a textual path into a waypoint list and turn actions, since LLM text-to-formal translation is easier in this form.

Two-extractor translation (Algorithm 1): separate LLM prompts extract waypoints with left-turn points and waypoints with right-turn points. If the waypoint lists differ, the extraction is retried up to C times, and a TurnPointChecker LLM resolves points flagged by both extractors.
Path finding: Dijkstra (shortest by edge count) on the topological map between the queried start and destination.
Action inference: for unstored turns, use an action algebra (inverse for reversal, e.g. L^-1=R; composition a(e_ji,e_ik)=a(e_ji,e_im)·T·a(e_mi,e_ik)) to derive actions.
Instruction generation: an LLM converts the resulting canonical path back into a natural-language instruction. Implemented with OpenAI GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 function calling.
Implicit baseline: put all the paths in the LLM prompt and ask directly for the reverse or combined path.

setting.backbone: GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 (frozen, prompted via function calling) plus a symbolic graph search
setting.action_space: output is a text path instruction with waypoints and Forward/Left/Right/Turn-around actions (no robot control)
setting.simulator: none; manual topological graphs built for 10 Matterport3D environments, with manually written path instructions
setting.privileged: none at test time; the user is assumed to give correct, complete, minimal-node paths with consistent node names

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 paths (10 environments x 10 textual paths), the authors' own dataset
numbers.evidence: Table I, Success rate of reverse paths evaluation: Explicit method GPT-4 94%

numbers.eval_set_note: 10 environments x 10 held-out paths, each generated from the other 9 input paths
numbers.evidence: Table II, Success rate of combined paths evaluation: Explicit method GPT-4 92% / 92%

numbers_note: No standard VLN benchmark is used; results are on the authors' own small dataset. Implicit baselines are omitted from numbers as baselines: reverse 67 (GPT-3.5) and 66 (GPT-4); combined 19/8 and 44/10.
results: On the authors' 100-path dataset, the explicit map with GPT-4 reaches 94% on reverse paths and 92% on combined paths (reachable and shortest). The implicit GPT-4 baseline gets 66% on reverse paths and only 44% reachable / 10% shortest on combined paths.
limitations: Assumes clean input: single start-to-goal descriptions, consistent node names, no user errors or ambiguity, and no multi-point descriptions.
Evaluated only on small house-scale environments with manually created graphs and paths; scalability to large spaces such as malls is untested.
Remaining failures come from LLM extraction errors of waypoints and turns; only turn-level (4-way) actions are modeled, with no metric geometry or real robot.
